extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and history of science (readers of Bacon / Novum Organum)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and cautions for sound natural philosophy/scientific method as discussed in Bacon's Novum Organum and commentary: what practices, assumptions, and demonstrations to avoid or adopt when investigating nature. Focuses on experiments, causes, authorities, abstractions, and intellectual idols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid twisting experience to fit preconceived decrees
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not decree first and then force experience to conform to those decrees (experientiam ad sua placita tortam circumducit et captivam).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: establishing axioms by fiat and afterward compelling observations to match them. The text criticises those who 'pri_us decreverat, neque experientiam ad constituenda decreta et axiomata rite consuluit; sed postquam pro arbitrio suo decrevisset, experientiam ad sua placita tortam circumducit et captivam.' Empirical investigation must be used to test and form doctrines, not to be tortured to justify preconceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require broad, repeated experimentation (not few, narrow experiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy built on the narrow confines of a few experiments produces 'deformia et monstrosa' opinions; frequent, limited experiments lead to false probabilistic certainty for some and incredulity for others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: empiric philosophies based on 'paucorum experimentorum angustiis et obscuritate' appear probable to those familiar with them but seem incredible to others. Experiments must be numerous, varied, and interpreted cautiously; avoid building general doctrines from sparse, local observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expunge superstition and theology from natural philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Corruption of philosophy occurs when superstition and theology are mixed into natural inquiries; natural phenomena should be referred to secondary (physical) causes rather than immediate divine action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: 'Bacon always insists on referring physical events to physical causes, and not ... to the immediate action of God.' The text advises that 'salutare admodum est, si mente sobria fidei tantum dentur quae fidei sunt.' Superstitious/theological admixture is 'pessima res' and leads to heretical religion and phantastic philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject occult qualities and specific virtues as explanatory endpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not invoke occult specific qualities as explanations for manifest effects; they stop the improvement of natural philosophy because they explain nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: telling us every species has an 'occult specific quality' is to tell us nothing. Instead, derive two or three general principles from phenomena and explain how properties and actions follow from those principles, leaving causes of those principles to be investigated later ('to derive two or three general principles of motion from phaenomena ... would be a very great step').

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer material and efficient causes for physics; relegate final/formal causes to metaphysics
rubrics_metrics.description: Physics should investigate material and efficient causes (the 'principia per quae'); final and formal causes belong properly to metaphysics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasises that for practical purposes it is more important to ask how a thing may be produced than what it is. Bacon specifies Material and Efficient Causes as appropriate for Physics and Final and Formal Causes as metaphysical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to intermediate (media) axioms, not only ultimate principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not neglect intermediate axioms; practical application of science usually depends on axiomata media rather than only the highest generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: 'The fifth and last error ... consists in the neglect of intermediate axioms, and the excessive attention paid to the principles of things and the ultimate constitution of nature.' Practical utility often comes from these middle-level generalisations, which must also be verifiable and fact-based ('talia scilicet, quae non abstracta sint, sed per haec media vere limitantur').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive abstraction to extremes (potential matter or atom) without practical value
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not abstract nature away to either pure potential matter or down to the atom as ends in themselves when those abstractions provide little help to human affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: 'abstrahere naturam ... donee ad materiam potentialem et informem ventum fuerit; nee rursus secare naturam desinant, donee perventum fuerit ad atomum; quae, etiamsi vera essent, tamen ad juvandas hominum fortunas parum possunt.' High abstractions are legitimate but must be grounded and useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use authorities as auxiliaries, not as substitutes for sense and inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Authority and received opinions should be neither wholly derided nor uncritically accepted; they are aids to, not replacements for, sensory observation and investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text: 'sensui et intellectui humano eorumque infirmitati authoritas non est deroganda, sed auxilia prebenda.' Authorities can support inquiry but must not obstruct investigation into nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid both dogmatism and extreme scepticism in philosophical assent
rubrics_metrics.description: Steer a middle course: shun the dogmatic positivism that pronounces final decrees and the acataleptic/infinite-inquiry stance that prevents definite conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast: Aristotle's dogmatism makes things 'certa et decreta' while Platonism/New Academy acatalepsia introduces endless inquiry. The recommended stance is measured assent: neither absolute dogma that crushes intellect nor perpetual doubt that enervates it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not derive nature's forms or principles from mechanical arts analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid inferring universal natural forms (primary forms, elementary qualities) simply because similar processes occur in mechanical arts; this leads to erroneous hypotheses (e.g., fictional 'elementary qualities').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: transferring notions from 'artibus mechanicis' to nature produced the fiction of elementary qualities and the hypothesis of primary forms. The commentator warns that such analogies produce 'inania contemplativa compendia' and mislead natural philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate true causes of motion rather than relying on popular divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Superficial popular divisions (generation, composition, augmentation, diminution, alteration, and 'lation') are mere measures/periods and do not penetrate into real causes or kinds of motion; inquiry should ask how, whence, and by what source motion arises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticises 'mere popular' divisions that only indicate that something is different without explaining the mode or source. Instead, seek principles that reveal causes (e.g., efficient causes, affinities, attractions) rather than accept folk categories as explanatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renounce the idols and false demonstrations that enslave thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellect must be purged of idols (mental idols) and 'pravae demonstrationes' which act as fortifications of error and bind human thought to technical vocabulary and preconception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: 'idola ... constanti et solenni decreto sunt abneganda et renuncianda, et intellectus ab iis omnino liberandus est et expurgandus.' Demonstrations that convert the world into managed thoughts and bind thinking to words ('enslaving the world to their own thoughts') are to be rejected; avoid technical terminologies and perverse laws of demonstration that cover false theories (idola theatri).
